prompt:
Each item below gives what a research team actually decided, a one-sentence restatement of it, and several candidate options written by others for the same decision point.

For each item answer:
- "faithful": "yes" if the restatement describes the same decision as what the team decided (abstracting away study-specific details is fine), "no" if it changes, drops the core of, or adds to the decision.
- "same": for each candidate label, "same" if the candidate is essentially the team's decision (a reader who knew what the team did would say the team took this option, or it contains the team's decision as a part), else "different".

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "faithful": "yes" | "no", "same": {"<label>": "same" | "different"}}]}

ITEMS:

=== key f2a2f8f41659
What the team decided: He challenges the claim that BIG-bench is a final AGI benchmark, noting PaLM already beats average humans on many tasks, the multiple-choice format favors LMs, and training-data leakage is likely.
Restatement: Challenge the claim that surpassing top human scores on this benchmark makes a model an AGI, and point out that an existing large model already beats average humans on many tasks.
C1: Claim only that surpassing top human scores would show strong performance on these written text tasks, and state that it falls short of establishing general intelligence.
C2: Claim that surpassing the top human score on this benchmark is a sufficient test of AGI, and announce any model that does so as an AGI without requiring further evaluations.

=== key a6286428c9dc
What the team decided: They did not test forecasting, keeping the paper focused on expressing the model's own uncertainty in natural language rather than improving forecasting ability.
Restatement: Do not extend the work to judgmental forecasting; keep the paper focused on having the model express its own uncertainty in natural language rather than on improving forecasting.
C1: Run a small pilot first, fine-tuning on resolved past forecasting questions and testing on held-out later questions, and compare calibration against base rates.
C2: Fine-tune the model directly on live forecasting platform questions using resolved outcomes as labels, and deploy it on open questions to see whether calibration carries over.

=== key b94354d8a074
What the team decided: He suggests testing whether GPT-3 can regenerate parts of well-known datasets like Iris, and adding finetuning, InstructGPT and embedding analyses.
Restatement: Prompt the model to regenerate parts of well-known public datasets that likely appeared in its training data, to check whether its in-context fitting reflects memorization.
C1: Test on synthetic functions with freshly sampled random parameters and unusual forms unlikely in training text, and compare the model against standard fitting baselines.
C2: Treat accurate predictions on a few new synthetic regression tasks as sufficient evidence of genuine in-context fitting and report the ability without a memorization test.

=== key d1619c3f0c2a
What the team decided: Recommends a wider distribution over future results and using base rates from how benchmarks improve after their introduction (e.g. plotting many benchmarks).
Restatement: Use a wider distribution over future results, and calibrate it with base rates from plotting how many other benchmarks improved after they were first introduced.
C1: Set wide uncertainty intervals, put substantial probability on rapid gains from better prompting, chain-of-thought and scale, and avoid anchoring on the weak early scores.
C2: Extrapolate from the weak early scores with a narrow interval, forecasting that performance stays low for several years and that gains need new methods rather than more scale.

=== key 1ec04a501059
What the team decided: Suggests measuring GPT-3's level across many foreign languages and comparing to known human time-to-proficiency as a benchmark.
Restatement: Measure the language model's proficiency across many foreign languages and compare it with the known time humans take to reach a given level in a foreign language.
C1: Run a controlled study with many participants trained over weeks, scored by log loss on the same text as language models, and compare learning curves against several model sizes.
C2: Treat the informal game result as sufficient evidence that language models out-predict humans on next-word prediction and cite it without running a larger study.

=== key d2011e93e85c
What the team decided: Reframes the evaluation around the main question of interest and asks how the results update beliefs on it, acknowledging both explanations remain possible.
Restatement: Frame the evaluation around the question of how well a transformer can do RL in context, and ask how this paper updates beliefs on it, with both explanations still possible.
C1: Update only slightly toward transformers doing strong in-context RL, treating the paper as narrow evidence and waiting for follow-up work that rules out the simpler explanations.
C2: Update substantially toward transformers being able to do strong in-context RL, and expect follow-up work to extend the result to broader and harder task settings.

=== key 157bd266e02d
What the team decided: Recommends comparing them on the actual distribution of queries sent to Google rather than on programmer-style examples.
Restatement: Compare the two tools on the actual distribution of queries people send to the web search engine rather than on programmer-style examples such as algorithm questions.
C1: Compare both tools on a sampled set of real user queries split by query type, with blind raters scoring answer correctness, verifiability and usefulness against sources.
C2: Try both tools on a handful of personally chosen queries and judge which one gives the more useful answer, without blinding or a formal rating rubric for scoring.

=== key 0f26859f55b5
What the team decided: Points to Galactica's limited benefits as evidence that curated-data training is less useful than training on a bigger dataset plus techniques to access the scientific parts.
Restatement: Train on a bigger dataset and use other techniques to make the model access the scientific parts of it, rather than training only on curated scientific text.
C1: Train matched small models on curated scientific text and on a size-matched random web sample, then compare benchmark performance across several model scales.
C2: Pretrain a large model mainly on curated scientific text and release it as a smarter model if it beats a standard web-trained model on a few popular benchmarks.

=== key 1a79aed6f2c3
What the team decided: Asks for overall accuracy (informative*truthful) for the unsteered base model with different prompts, and for positive and negative steering.
Restatement: Report overall accuracy combining informativeness and truthfulness on the benchmark for the unsteered model under different prompts and under positive and negative steering.
C1: Sweep steering magnitude across a wide range with confidence intervals, and report truthfulness gains next to held-out capability benchmark scores at every magnitude.
C2: Report the headline truthfulness gain at one steering magnitude and claim steering reduces sycophancy, leaving the magnitude sweep and capability checks for later work.

=== key 949e3b1a3c20
What the team decided: Suggests an ablation using random steering vectors (e.g. love/hate, big/small) as a control.
Restatement: Run an ablation that steers with random unrelated vectors, such as love versus hate or big versus small, and compare the effect against the sycophancy vector.
C1: Compare the sycophancy vector against several random vectors of matched norm and an unrelated-trait steering vector, measuring truthfulness change for each control.
C2: Treat the truthfulness gain as evidence of sycophancy-specific steering after a single random-vector control of matched norm shows no comparable improvement.

=== key da67b04c2988
What the team decided: Accepted the variation as typical of scaling results and ran a replication on a disjoint set of tasks to check the claims generalize.
Restatement: Accept the task-to-task variation as typical of scaling results and run a replication of the main experiment on a disjoint set of tasks to check the claims generalize.

=== key bc1761609a48
